# Summary of Scottish National Party Manifesto 1997: "YES WE CAN — Win the Best for Scotland"

The 1997 SNP Manifesto presents a passionate case for Scottish independence, framed around the assertion that Scotland is a wealthy nation being held back by the Westminster Union. Led by Alex Salmond, the party argues that Scotland has been subsidising London rather than receiving subsidies—citing Treasury figures showing £27 billion more sent south than received since 1979—and that only independence can unlock Scotland's full potential.

## The Case for Independence

The manifesto directly challenges what it calls "smears and fears" from Labour and Conservatives, asserting that Scotland would automatically become an EU member upon independence, would have open borders with England, and would rank as the eighth richest developed nation when including North Sea resources. The SNP dismisses the "sterile, out of date and bankrupt political British system" and presents independence as the normal status for wealthy small nations, noting that nearly half of independent nations worldwide are smaller than Scotland.

## Constitutional Vision

An independent Scotland would feature a written constitution and Bill of Rights, transforming Scots from "subjects" to "citizens." The manifesto proposes a single-chamber parliament elected by proportional representation, extending voting rights to 16-year-olds, and abolishing the "mumbo jumbo of Royal assent." The House of Lords is dismissed as an institution based on "accident of birth or political patronage" with no place in modern democracy.

## Economic Programme

The SNP commits to reducing business taxation, including cutting corporation tax from 33p to 30p and the small companies rate by 22%. Personal taxation would favour lower and middle earners, with 85% of male employees and 95% of female employees paying less tax, while those earning above £26,500 would contribute slightly more—reflecting "basic Scottish belief in progressive taxation."

The manifesto targets full employment and pledges 100,000 new jobs through enterprise development, export promotion, and tourism expansion. It commits to taking Railtrack into public ownership and establishing a Scottish skills foundation.

## Social Justice

Central to the SNP's vision is comprehensive social provision: increasing Child Benefit, restoring benefits to 16-17 year olds, and implementing a "Pensioners Package" including pension increases and abolishing means-testing for elderly care. The manifesto promises abolition of the NHS internal market, additional health spending, and free nursery education while restoring student maintenance grants.

On housing, the manifesto pledges to transfer local authority housing debt to central government, releasing £1.6 billion for investment to build 20,000 affordable homes and eliminate homelessness.

## Defence and International Relations

Scotland would establish appropriate defence forces, restore traditional regiments, and crucially negotiate the complete withdrawal of Trident nuclear weapons from the Clyde. The SNP proposes phased withdrawal from NATO while maintaining European security cooperation. The manifesto commits to reaching the UN's 0.7% GDP target for international aid within six years.

## Conclusion

The manifesto concludes with a fully-costed four-year budget demonstrating fiscal responsibility while delivering transformative change. The SNP positions independence not as separation but as Scotland joining the community of nations, playing its full part in Europe and the world while caring properly for its citizens—capturing this in the repeated refrain: "If the SNP wins, so does Scotland."
